sections.html:
It's a break on the school operating part of your property tax bill. The exemption removes the local school operating millage, up to 18 mills, from the bill of an owner's principal residence. The statute behind it is MCL 211.7cc.

People often call it the homestead exemption, but Michigan keeps two ideas apart. The Homestead Property Tax Credit is a separate credit claimed on an income tax return. The exemption covered here is claimed with the local assessor and shows up on the tax roll.

A principal residence is the one place where an owner has a true, fixed and permanent home to which the owner intends to return whenever absent. It also reaches unoccupied residential or timber-cutover land next to the dwelling that the owner owns and occupies (MCL 211.7dd(c)).

Only an individual with a documented ownership interest. Verbal agreements create no interest, and the person claiming carries the burden of proof. These owners are eligible:

  • A person who owns the property, including a partial owner.
  • A land contract purchaser under a written contract that the seller signed.
  • A holder of a life estate, who is treated as a partial owner.
  • A beneficiary who receives ownership rights under a will, a trust, or intestate succession.
  • A grantor who placed the home in a revocable trust or a qualified personal residence trust.
  • A cooperative housing corporation or a registered life care facility.

An LLC, a corporation, a shareholder of a corporation, and a sole member of an LLC don't qualify. A trust isn't itself an owner, though its grantor or beneficiaries may be. A married couple filing a joint Michigan return gets only one exemption (MCL 211.7cc(3)).

sections.h2: Where and when to file the affidavit
sections.html:
File Form 2368, the Principal Residence Exemption Affidavit, with the assessor for the city or township where the home sits. The statute sets June 1 for the summer levy and November 1 for the winter levy (MCL 211.7cc(2)). A valid affidavit filed by June 1 reduces that year's bill starting with the summer levy. One filed from June 2 through November 1 reduces it starting with the winter levy.

The affidavit swears that you own and occupy the property on the signing date and haven't claimed a substantially similar break in another state. Claiming both brings a $500 penalty. A false claim can also bring perjury charges, with penalties that include up to a year in jail and fines of $1,000 to $5,000 (MCL 211.120).

Closing agents and local assessors hand out the forms, and Treasury posts them too. A closing statement preparer who skips the forms isn't legally liable for that, so the seller and buyer should ask for them.

You can still file. File Form 2368 with the local assessor at any time during the year. The assessor may grant the exemption back through the current year and the three years before it, provided you met the requirements on June 1 or November 1 of each year claimed. If the owner has died, the estate can file for the same period.

The July and December Boards of Review no longer have authority to grant late claims. Only the assessor does, so go to the assessor's office instead of waiting for a board hearing.

sections.h2: Two parcels, a duplex or a split lot
sections.html:
Each parcel needs its own affidavit. If your home sits on one parcel and contiguous residential land is a second parcel, both need Form 2368. When a parcel is split or combined, the new parcel numbers call for a fresh affidavit.

If the home is one unit of a multiple-unit dwelling, or a dwelling within a mixed-use building, you claim only the share of taxable value used as your principal residence, in the manner Treasury prescribes (MCL 211.7cc(16)). A landlord who lives in one side of a duplex therefore claims that side only. Ask the local assessor how the portion is measured before you file.

sections.h2: What a seller must do with the exemption
sections.html:
The exemption lasts until December 31 of the year the property is transferred, or until it stops being a principal residence (MCL 211.7cc(4)). Within 90 days after you stop using the home as your principal residence, file Form 2602 with the local tax collecting unit. Rescission is still required in several cases: the owner dies, a spouse leaves after a divorce, or the owner moves out during a foreclosure redemption period.

There's one holding option if you moved and the house is for sale. An owner who claims the exemption on a new current residence can keep it on the old home for up to 3 tax years by filing a conditional rescission form, as long as the old home is unoccupied, listed for sale, not leased, and not used for business. Lease it and the local unit denies the conditional rescission back to the prior December 31.

An owner who moved into a nursing home or assisted living facility may keep the exemption if the home stays owned, no new principal residence is set up, the home is maintained, and it isn't leased or used for business.

An assessor who believes the home isn't the owner's principal residence can deny a new or existing claim in writing, for the current year and up to the three years before. The owner has 35 days from the notice date to appeal to the residential and small claims division of the Michigan tax tribunal, and doesn't have to pay the disputed tax to appeal. Counties can elect to audit claims, and Treasury audits annually in counties that don't.

Back taxes carry interest at 1.25% per month or fraction of a month from the date they were last payable without penalty. If the home was sold to a bona fide purchaser before the extra bill went out, the tax, interest and penalties aren't a lien on the property and aren't billed to that buyer. Treasury assesses the former owner instead. That protection is one reason to rescind promptly.

A land contract buyer has one more filing: a Property Transfer Affidavit, Form 2766, with the local assessor within 45 days of the transfer.

sections.h2: Before you list: a seller's checklist
sections.html:
Run through this list a few weeks before you put the house on the market, or before you accept a cash offer.

  • Find out whether an affidavit is on file for each parcel you own.
  • Pick your move-out date and mark 90 days from it for Form 2602.
  • If you're buying another home first, ask the assessor about the conditional rescission for the house you're selling.
  • Give the buyer a copy of the transfer affidavit requirement so they can file within 45 days of the transfer.

A fast cash closing doesn't change these deadlines. The exemption still ends on December 31 of the year of transfer, and the buyer starts their own claim by filing Form 2368 once they own and occupy the home.

faqs.q: Does Michigan's exemption cover the whole property tax bill?
faqs.a: No. It removes the local school operating millage, up to 18 mills. Other millages still apply, so a bill drops but doesn't vanish.

faqs.q: Can I claim it on a cottage with a higher taxable value than my house?
faqs.a: No. The exemption is only for the property that is your true, fixed and permanent home, never for the sake of potential tax savings.

faqs.q: Do I have to file a new affidavit every year?
faqs.a: No. A valid claim stays on the property while the owner keeps meeting the requirements. A new affidavit is needed when a parcel is split or combined, because that creates new parcel numbers.

faqs.q: Who files the rescission when an owner dies?
faqs.a: The estate's personal representative or trustee files Form 2602 with the assessor within 90 days of death, because the deceased owner can no longer occupy the home or intend to return.

faqs.q: What if my trust owns the house?
faqs.a: The grantor or beneficiary who lives there signs Form 2368 in their own name, with the trust role noted. If the grantor can't sign, the trustee may sign on the grantor's behalf.
